request.system:
You assist an automated astronomer who infers how a body moves from angles-only sky observations (ecliptic longitude/latitude seen from an observer whose orbit is known). Jan, the fitting engine, fits candidate model families by least squares and compares them by Bayesian evidence. You see numerical summaries of the current best fit and its residuals, and you propose the next candidates to fit.

A candidate is either a registered family (by exact name) or a new central force law: the radial acceleration f(r) in AU/day^2 (negative = attractive) as an expression in r (heliocentric distance, AU), GM (the Sun's, 2.959e-4 AU^3/day^2, fixed) and parameters you declare with bounds and an initial value. Allowed in expressions: numbers, + - * / **, parentheses, exp, log, sqrt, tanh, pi, r, GM and your parameter names (lowercase, letters/digits/underscore). Prefer the simplest law that explains the residual structure; a new parameter must buy a clear improvement. Reply "stop": true when the residuals are consistent with noise or further candidates are unlikely to help.

parsed.analysis: The free power law (n≈1.75, C≈0.77 GM) is far ahead of the other candidates, but it is not a good description. The noise sigma was fitted, so rms/sigma=1 says nothing about fit quality, and an rms of about 2.5° is enormous. The residuals are also strongly structured. A single periodogram peak at 343 d (power 0.91) sits at exactly half the ~685 d orbital period, which points to a mismatch in orbital shape or in how the force varies around the orbit. The time-binned east residuals swing by up to ±8000″. The two half-span ellipse fits show a large retrograde apsidal shift of about −39° per orbit. That is consistent with n<2, i.e. an effective force that falls off more slowly than 1/r² over the narrow 1.37–1.52 AU range. The distance-binned means show no clean trend, so the structure may be partly non-radial or time-dependent. An unseen perturbing planet is untested and could produce harmonic structure like this, so I propose perturbed-conic. I also propose Yukawa for completeness, although a screened Yukawa force would give prograde rather than retrograde precession, so it is a long shot. Finally, I propose a two-term radial law that keeps a near-Newtonian core with a free mass scale and adds a slowly falling 1/r term. Over the small distance range it mimics n_eff<2, and unlike the pure power law it can change how the force varies around the orbit.

proposals.rationale: Strong half-orbital-period residual structure and large time-dependent east swings could come from an unseen perturber rather than a modified central law; untested so far.
Untested single-parameter modification of Newtonian gravity; worth checking, although it would give prograde rather than the observed retrograde precession, so it is a long shot.

The free power law prefers C≈0.77 GM and n≈1.75, and the precession is retrograde. A scaled 1/r² term plus a slowly falling 1/r term reproduces n_eff<2 with two parameters, and it may fit the half-period residual harmonic better than a single power law.
